newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian investment boom gives economy a push.
newsitem.headline: Australian investment boom gives economy a push.

text.p: Australian business investment is booming, particularly in the mining and telecommunications sectors, and this should ensure economic growth accelerates in 1997 after a modest slowdown this year, analysts said on Monday.

Capital expenditure figures released on Monday by the Bureau of Statistics suggested investment would even outstrip the government's budget forecast of 14 percent for 1996/97 - a forecast which had been considered overly optimistic by many.
However, economists said the news appeared to lengthen odds against another interest rate cut in the near term.
"This was a crucial result," said Tony Meer, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Investment had to maintain the momentum built up in 1995/96 and, however you cut it, it has."
"In fact, it even suggests Treasury may have been a little conservative with their forecast, and who would have thought that a week ago?" he said.
Treasurer Peter Costello, commenting on the figures, also appeared to suggest he favoured holding off on rates.

Asked if he felt business could use another rate cut after cuts in July and early November, Costello told reporters: "This has been a very good result. Let's just let those interest rates work themselves through the economic system."
Official interest rates stand at 6.5 percent following two cuts of 0.5 percentage points.
Analysts said that while strength in investment diminished the chances of another easing in official interest rates it did not completely rule out a move during the first quarter of 1997.

"The thing is, the growth in investment is mostly in sectors which are not employment intensive, like telecoms and mining," said Meer. "So if you have concerns about jobs growth, like the RBA has, there may be a case for another rate cut to boost the sectors that are, like retail," he said.
Australia's unemployment rate stands at 8.8 percent.
The Bureau of Statistics said private new capital expenditure (capex) rose 0.9 percent in the September quarter, seasonally adjusted, on the quarter before.
This was a robust result given that capex had jumped 13.2 percent in the June quarter and it was well above market forecasts which had centred on a 3.0 percent fall.
Analysts were particularly surprised by a 2.4 percent rise in plant and equipment spending, which did not seem to gell with imports of capital goods which fell sharply in the period.
This alone was likely to add about 0.15 percentage point to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth for the quarter, they said.

"It's positive that the surprise was in plant and equipment spending," said Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP Investments. "It suggests you're probably going to see a positive contribution to growth from business investment."
Equally important was the latest survey of investment intentions for the whole 1996/97 year which showed industry was even more upbeat than the government.

The fourth forecast for 1996/97 -- the ABS takes six surveys in all starting in the December quarter of the previous fiscal year -- was for spending of A$42.91 billion (US$34.75 billion), a 19.2 percent rise on the fourth estimate for 1995/96.

Assuming expectations turn into actual investment at the average ratio of the past five years, the forecast points to spending of A$44.20 billion in 1996/97. That would be a rise of 15.3 percent on the A$38.34 billion recorded for 95/96, which itself represented an annual increase of 11.7 percent.
This bodes well for the economy since investment makes up about 15 percent of GDP and a result close to expectations would add about 2.0 percentage points to growth in 1996/97.
"The surprising strength in the expectations for 1996/97 is underpinning the good growth story," said Matthew Drennan, an economist at Axiom Funds Management.
Analysts reckoned the government's budget time forecast of 3.5 percent GDP growth in 1996/97 now looked a lot more reasonable than it had just a month ago.
It would also be a relief to the Reserve Bank which had called investment the "linchpin of forecast growth."
